common_diseases.name: Late blight
common_diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaves and fruit, white fungal growth
common_diseases.treatment: Apply copper-based fungicides and use resistant varieties

common_diseases.name: Early blight
common_diseases.symptoms: Target-shaped lesions on lower leaves, yellowing
common_diseases.treatment: Rotate crops, apply fungicide sprays such as chlorothalonil

common_diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
common_diseases.treatment: Use resistant cultivars and soil solarization

common_pests.name: Tomato fruit worm (Helicoverpa armigera)
common_pests.treatment: Biological control with Bacillus thuringiensis, pheromone traps

common_pests.name: Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
common_pests.treatment: Insecticidal soap, neem oil, reflective mulches

common_pests.name: Aphids (Myzus persicae)
common_pests.treatment: Introduce lady beetles, use insecticidal soap

crop_profile.summary: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is an annual fruit crop thriving in warm, humid climates with 18-30°C temperatures, 60-80% humidity, and 500-1000 mm annual rainfall. It prefers loam soils, pH 5.5-7.0, good drainage, and high nitrogen. Drip irrigation, balanced NPK (10-10-10) and organic amendments boost yields of 60-90 t/ha. Major producers include China, India, USA, Turkey, and Egypt. Key challenges are late blight, early blight, Fusarium wilt, and pests like fruit worm, whitefly, and aphids. Proper irrigation, fertilization, timely harvest, and refrigerated storage ensure high-quality marketable fruit.

recommendation.recommendation: Apply nitrogen fertilizer to correct low soil nitrogen levels
recommendation.justification: Soil analysis shows nitrogen is low, while tomatoes require a high nitrogen supply for optimal vegetative growth and yield. All other conditions (soil texture, pH, organic carbon, moisture) are favorable, and satellite NDVI indicates excellent crop vigor, providing a strong opportunity to boost productivity without additional irrigation. Addressing the nitrogen deficit now will prevent yield loss and capitalize on the current market stability.
actions: Confirm current soil nitrogen level with a quick field nitrate test (e.g., colorimetric kit).
Select a high‑N fertilizer (e.g., urea 46% N or calcium nitrate) appropriate for drip‑fertigation.
Apply the recommended nitrogen rate (≈100 kg N ha⁻¹) split into two doses: first dose within the next 3 days, second dose at the onset of flowering.
Deliver the fertilizer through the existing drip system to ensure uniform distribution and minimize leaching.
Record application date, amount, and method in the farm log.
recommendation.expected_outcome: Restored nitrogen balance will enhance vegetative growth, improve fruit set, and increase total marketable yield, leading to higher profitability while maintaining soil health.
monitoring_plan: Weekly visual scouting for nitrogen deficiency symptoms (pale leaves, reduced growth).
Measure leaf chlorophyll content (SPAD meter) weekly; target values >45 for tomatoes.
Track NDVI from satellite or drone imagery every 7‑10 days; maintain values ≥0.65.
Re‑test soil nitrate 2 weeks after the first application to verify uptake and adjust the second dose if needed.
Observe for any signs of over‑fertilization (leaf burn, excessive vegetative growth) and adjust future rates accordingly.
